title: The golden ratio
examples: Is the golden ratio only found in nature?
How did artists actually calculate the golden ratio?
Can you show me an example of the golden ratio in architecture?

explain.say: Today we are learning about a special number called the golden ratio.

items: The golden ratio is approximately 1 point 618.
It is represented by the Greek letter phi, or \phi.
It appears in many natural and artistic designs.

explain.say: A golden rectangle is a shape where the ratio of its sides is the golden ratio.
When you draw a golden spiral inside a golden rectangle, it grows outwards in a pleasing curve.
Nature often uses this ratio to create beautiful and efficient growth patterns.
Artists have used the golden ratio to create compositions that are pleasing to the human eye.
In everyday life, you see this ratio in things like the proportions of shells or even some building designs.

faq.q: Is the golden ratio the same as the Fibonacci sequence?
faq.a: They are closely related, but they are not exactly the same thing. The Fibonacci sequence generates numbers that approach the golden ratio.
asks: What is the link between phi and Fibonacci?
Do I need both numbers to understand this?

faq.q: Does everything in nature follow the golden ratio?
faq.a: No, while many things show approximations of it, nature is complex and not every single object follows this exact mathematical rule.
asks: Are there exceptions to the golden ratio?

faq.q: Is this ratio only important for art?
faq.a: No, it is also very important in mathematics, physics, and biology for understanding natural growth patterns.
asks: Is it used in engineering too?

faq.q: If I use the golden ratio, will my art automatically look good?
faq.a: It is a guideline, not a magic formula. Using it can help create balance, but your own creativity is what makes the art special.
asks: Is this a guarantee of beauty?
Should I always use this ratio?

faq.q: What is the actual value of the golden ratio?
faq.a: The exact value is represented by the Greek letter phi, which is approximately 1 point 618.
asks: Can you write the number out?

facts: The golden ratio, $\phi$, is an irrational number.
It is often approximated by the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
A golden rectangle has the property that a square cut from it leaves another golden rectangle.
The spiral formed by connecting the corners of squares in a golden rectangle is the golden spiral.

quiz.say: If a rectangle has sides of 10 and 16 point 18, what is the ratio of the longer side to the shorter side?
quiz.why: The definition of the golden rectangle is that the ratio of its sides equals the golden ratio, 1 point 618.

wrong.0: This is the sum of the two sides, not the ratio.
wrong.1: This would only be true if the rectangle was a square.
wrong.2: This is just the length of the longer side.

quiz.say: Which mathematical sequence is most closely related to the golden ratio?
quiz.why: The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers gets closer and closer to the golden ratio.

wrong.0: Prime numbers are only divisible by one and themselves.
wrong.1: This involves adding the same number each time, not multiplying by increasing ratios.
wrong.3: These triples deal with right-angled triangles, not sequential ratios.

quiz.say: If you divide a golden rectangle into a square and a smaller rectangle, what is the ratio of the smaller rectangle to the original?
quiz.why: The smaller rectangle remaining after cutting a square always maintains the golden ratio.

wrong.1: This would mean the smaller rectangle was a square itself.
wrong.2: The ratio decreases, it does not increase by squaring.
wrong.3: The relationship is multiplicative, not simply dividing by two.
